items.prompt: Course P must be completed before course Q. Which directed edge orientation supports Kahn's topological processing?

options.text: Q → P, because Q names P as a prerequisite.
Use an undirected edge because dependency is just connectivity.
P → Q, so completing P removes one unmet prerequisite from Q.
Add both P → Q and Q → P so the relationship is visible in either direction.

feedback.reason: Edges point from a prerequisite to the work it unlocks, matching indegree as the count of unmet prerequisites.

blocks.text: Point from the prerequisite to what it unlocks

items: Represent “P before Q” as edge P → Q.
That edge contributes one to indegree[Q], so Q begins with one unmet prerequisite.
P has no prerequisite from this relation and may become ready first.
When P is processed, traverse P → Q and decrement indegree[Q].

blocks.text: Reversing the edge would make processing Q unlock P, the opposite schedule. Adding both directions claims mutual dependency and creates a cycle; an undirected edge loses precedence entirely.

blocks.title: Orientation rule
blocks.text: prerequisite → dependent makes indegree equal the number of unmet prerequisites.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.q_to_p: That orientation makes processing Q reduce P's indegree and reverses the prerequisite effect.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both: The two-edge representation creates a directed cycle and says each course depends on the other.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.undirected: A prerequisite has direction; undirected reachability cannot encode which item must precede the other.

items.prompt: Which vertices belong in the initial queue of Kahn's algorithm for a directed dependency graph?

options.text: One arbitrary vertex, because ordinary BFS always starts from one source.
Every vertex whose indegree is zero, including isolated vertices.
All vertices, with visited marking deferred until dequeue.
Only the vertex with the most outgoing edges, because it unlocks the most work.

feedback.reason: Indegree zero is the exact readiness predicate, and every currently ready vertex may be processed.

blocks.text: Seed every item that is ready now

items: indegree[v] counts v's currently unmet incoming prerequisites.
Every vertex with indegree 0 is immediately legal to process.
An isolated vertex has no incoming edges, so it is also ready even though no traversal reaches it from another vertex.

blocks.text: Kahn's queue is a global ready set, not a single-source reachability frontier. Choosing only one arbitrary or highest-outdegree vertex can omit independent ready work; inserting all vertices would publish dependents whose prerequisites remain unmet.

blocks.title: Initial frontier
blocks.text: Enqueue all and only zero-indegree vertices.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_arbitrary: Dependency processing may have several independent ready items; omitting them can leave a valid DAG unprocessed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_vertices: Vertices with unmet prerequisites are not ready and must not enter the processing queue.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.highest_outdegree: Readiness is determined by zero unmet prerequisites, not by a greedy outdegree preference.

items.prompt: Vertex u has already been removed from Kahn's ready queue and appended to the output. For one outgoing edge u → v, order the dependent-state transitions that publish v exactly when its final prerequisite is satisfied.

elements.text: Decrement indegree[v] for the satisfied edge u → v.
Test whether indegree[v] has just become zero.
If it became zero, enqueue v in the ready queue.

feedback.reason: Readiness is evaluated after the current prerequisite decrement, and publication occurs only on the transition to zero.

blocks.text: Publish v on the transition to zero

items: Decrement indegree[v] because processed prerequisite u has satisfied edge u → v.
Inspect the new value.
If and only if it is zero, enqueue v once as newly ready.

blocks.text: If indegree[v] changes from 2 to 1, another prerequisite remains and v must stay out of the queue. If it changes from 1 to 0, every prerequisite has now been processed. Testing before decrement misses this event; enqueuing without the zero test publishes too early or repeatedly.

blocks.title: Readiness transition
blocks.text: decrement → test new value → enqueue exactly on zero.

items.prompt: A DAG initially has two zero-indegree vertices A and B, and neither depends on the other. What does their presence imply about the topological order?

options.text: A must appear first because it was listed first in the input.
BFS queue semantics make the topological order mathematically unique.
Two initial ready vertices prove there is a cycle between them.
Either may appear first; the graph can have multiple valid topological orders.

feedback.reason: A topological order constrains only dependency-related pairs; incomparable ready vertices may be ordered either way.

blocks.text: Incomparable ready vertices create valid tie choices

With no path or edge constraint ordering A against B, both have zero indegree. Choosing A then B or B then A preserves every existing dependency, so both prefixes can belong to valid topological orders.

items: A FIFO queue selects one order from insertion order.
A priority queue can select a lexicographically smallest ready vertex.
Neither policy makes the mathematical order unique.

blocks.title: Uniqueness signal
blocks.text: A Kahn run has a unique next choice only when the ready set contains exactly one vertex at that step.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a_must_first: Input order is not a dependency unless an edge or explicit tie policy says so.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_unique: FIFO preserves a chosen insertion order, but another valid tie order can produce another legal result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.cycle: Zero indegree means neither currently has an incoming prerequisite; it does not imply a cycle.

items.prompt: Kahn's algorithm finishes after outputting 7 of 9 declared vertices. What is the decisive conclusion?

options.text: The two remaining vertices are merely in another disconnected DAG component.
The result only proves adjacency lists were used instead of a matrix.
At least one directed cycle prevents the remaining vertices from ever reaching indegree zero.
Marking vertices on dequeue would automatically process the missing two.

feedback.reason: A DAG always exposes at least one zero-indegree vertex in every remaining nonempty subgraph.

blocks.text: A nonempty DAG remainder must expose a ready vertex

Assume a finite nonempty directed remainder has no cycle. Following incoming edges backward cannot continue forever, so it must end at a vertex with no incoming edge inside that remainder. That vertex would have residual indegree zero and enter Kahn's queue.

Here the queue is empty after only 7 of V = 9 vertices, contradicting that DAG property. At least one directed cycle remains; vertices outside the cycle may also remain if they depend on it. Disconnected acyclic regions would have seeded their own zero-indegree vertices and been processed.

blocks.title: Cycle check
blocks.text: After Kahn processing, processedCount < V if and only if no complete topological order exists because a directed cycle remains.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.disconnected: All zero-indegree vertices from every component were seeded; a disconnected acyclic component would still be processed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_error: Both representations can support Kahn's algorithm; incomplete processing is a dependency-state signal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.late_visited: Kahn's admission is indegree zero, not ordinary visited timing; a cycle leaves no legal ready vertex.

items.prompt: Why is Kahn's algorithm not just ordinary single-source BFS with a different name?

options.text: It is ordinary BFS, but BFS is always faster than DFS so the name emphasizes speed.
Its queue admits every vertex when its remaining indegree becomes zero, not when first reached from one source.
It is not a graph algorithm because prerequisites form a tree.
It differs only because Kahn's algorithm requires an adjacency matrix.

feedback.reason: Kahn's frontier represents globally ready work, whereas BFS's frontier represents states reached at successive path lengths from sources.

blocks.text: The same container can serve a different invariant

items: Ordinary BFS admits a vertex when an edge first discovers it from a source-reachable frontier.
Kahn admits a vertex when its remaining indegree becomes zero, possibly without being reachable from one chosen start.
BFS layers encode unweighted distance; Kahn's queue encodes global dependency readiness.

blocks.text: Using first discovery for dependencies can publish a vertex after only one of several prerequisites. Requiring one source can omit independent DAG regions. FIFO is an implementation detail shared by two different state transitions.

blocks.title: Algorithm identity
blocks.text: Name an algorithm by its state invariant and admission rule, not by the container it uses.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_faster: The algorithms maintain different invariants; speed does not define Kahn processing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_graph: Dependency graphs can branch, converge, be disconnected, and contain cycles.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_only: Outgoing adjacency lists plus an indegree array are the standard O(V + E) representation.

items.prompt: A dependency DAG has two disconnected subgraphs and one isolated vertex. What must a complete topological-order implementation do?

options.text: Start from one arbitrary source and stop when its reachable component is exhausted.
Increment a component counter and treat the count as the topological order.
Add artificial edges between subgraphs so one BFS can reach all vertices.
Include zero-indegree vertices from every subgraph and the isolated vertex, producing an order of all declared vertices.

feedback.reason: Topological ordering covers the entire declared DAG, including independent components and isolated vertices.

blocks.text: Topological order covers the declared vertex set globally

items: Compute indegree for every declared vertex in both subgraphs and for the isolate.
Seed every zero-indegree vertex, including the isolated one.
Process readiness transitions independently across both subgraphs.
Accept the result only when the output contains all V declared vertices.

blocks.text: The isolated vertex has no constraints and may appear wherever the tie policy places it. Artificial links would change the set of valid orders; a single-source traversal would omit legal independent work.

blocks.title: Coverage rule
blocks.text: Kahn needs no component restarts because its initial and newly-ready queues are global over all declared vertices.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_component: That is single-source traversal and omits independent valid work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.new_component_count: Component identity does not order prerequisites within each directed subgraph.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.link_components: Artificial dependencies change the set of valid orders and the input problem.

items.prompt: For a sparse dependency graph, which representation and state support an O(V + E) Kahn implementation?

options.text: An adjacency matrix, because dependency order needs constant-time membership for every pair.
One parent pointer per vertex, because dependencies form a traversal tree.
Outgoing adjacency lists plus an indegree value for every declared vertex.
A visited set with marking on dequeue; indegrees are redundant.

feedback.reason: Kahn needs efficient outgoing-edge enumeration and an explicit remaining-prerequisite count.

blocks.text: Charge each vertex and dependency once

items: Initialize V adjacency-list headers and V indegree counters in O(V).
For each of E directed edges u → v, append v under u and increment indegree[v] once.
Each vertex enters and leaves the ready queue once, for O(V) queue work.
Processing outgoing lists decrements each edge exactly once, for O(E) work.

blocks.text: Total time and representation space are O(V + E). A matrix can represent the same graph but scans or stores V² pairs. One parent cannot encode converging prerequisites, and visited alone cannot report how many prerequisites remain.

blocks.title: Canonical state
blocks.text: Use outgoing adjacency lists plus one indegree counter for every declared vertex.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_required: Kahn repeatedly enumerates actual outgoing edges; sparse adjacency lists avoid scanning absent pairs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.parent_only: A dependent can have several prerequisites and a prerequisite can unlock several dependents.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.visited_only: Visited tracks processing but does not tell when all prerequisites of a vertex have been satisfied.

items.prompt: Kahn's algorithm processes a dependency graph but emits fewer vertices than exist. What does that establish?

options.text: The graph contains a directed cycle, so no complete topological order exists.
The queue needs to be sorted before continuing.
Every unprocessed vertex must be isolated.
BFS cannot be used on any directed graph.

feedback.reason: A cycle leaves every vertex in the cycle with a positive remaining indegree, so the zero-indegree frontier becomes empty early.

blocks.text: If all vertices are emitted, the order is a valid topological order. If emission stops early, the residual dependency constraints contain a cycle rather than merely an ordering inconvenience.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_unstable: Tie-breaking among zero-indegree vertices changes which valid order is chosen, not whether a cycle exists.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.edge_missing: Unprocessed vertices can still have incoming edges from the residual cyclic subgraph.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_failed: Kahn's algorithm uses a queue-like frontier but is specifically a topological-order procedure.

items.prompt: Which condition must hold for a directed graph to admit a topological ordering?

options.text: It must be a directed acyclic graph.
Every vertex must be reachable from one common source.
All directed edges must be replaceable by undirected edges.
Every vertex must have the same indegree and outdegree.

feedback.reason: A directed cycle would require each member to appear after its predecessor and before it at the same time.

blocks.text: Disconnected DAGs are valid: topological sorting can interleave independent components. Connectivity and balanced degrees are not requirements.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.connected: Independent components can each be ordered and then interleaved.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.undirected: Topological order is defined for directed precedence constraints.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.equal_degree: Degree balance is unrelated to the absence of directed cycles.

items.prompt: What does indegree[v] count before Kahn's algorithm starts?

options.text: The number of directed edges whose destination is v.
The number of dependencies v points to.
The number of vertices reachable from v.
The position at which v will be emitted.

feedback.reason: Kahn's frontier contains vertices with no remaining incoming prerequisites.

blocks.text: Initialize indegrees by counting each edge u->v at v. When u is emitted, decrement the indegree of its outgoing destinations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.outgoing_edges: Outgoing count is outdegree and does not measure prerequisites.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reachable_vertices: Reachability is not a local dependency count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.queue_position: Queue position is derived after indegrees are processed.

items.prompt: When Kahn's algorithm emits u, which neighbors become eligible for the frontier?

options.text: Outgoing neighbors whose remaining indegree becomes zero.
Every outgoing neighbor, regardless of other prerequisites.
Only vertices with edges into u.
The neighbor with the greatest outdegree only.

feedback.reason: Emitting u removes one prerequisite from each outgoing neighbor; zero means all prerequisites are satisfied.

blocks.text: Do not enqueue a vertex while it still has another incoming dependency. The frontier invariant is precisely zero remaining indegree.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_neighbors: Some neighbors may still depend on other unprocessed vertices.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.incoming_neighbors: Incoming neighbors are prerequisites that may already have been emitted.

items.prompt: How can DFS postorder produce a topological order in a DAG?

options.text: Append each vertex after its descendants finish, then reverse the finish list.
Return vertices in the order they are first discovered.
Sort vertices by outdegree after DFS.
Enqueue each edge and read the queue without a reverse.

feedback.reason: A dependency is finished before its predecessor; reversing finish order places predecessors first.

blocks.text: The DFS version also needs an active-stack cycle check. If a back edge is found, no topological order exists.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.discovery_order: Discovery order can place a dependent before an unprocessed prerequisite.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_degree: Degree is not the topological precedence relation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.queue_edges: Edge queue order does not establish descendant completion order.

items.prompt: What does an empty zero-indegree frontier mean at the start of Kahn's algorithm?

options.text: Either the graph has no vertices, or every remaining vertex is part of a dependency cycle.
The graph is definitely acyclic and the queue only needs sorting.
All source vertices have already been emitted even before processing starts.
The graph must be undirected.

feedback.reason: A nonempty DAG must contain at least one zero-indegree vertex; absence indicates cyclic dependency in the residual graph.

blocks.text: Handle the empty-graph case separately if the contract allows it. For a nonempty graph, an empty initial frontier is a direct cycle signal.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_dag: A DAG must expose at least one source vertex.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_sources_done: No vertex has been emitted yet at initialization.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.undirected_graph: Direction and cycles, not graph being undirected, determine indegree eligibility.

items.prompt: In Kahn's algorithm, what does the zero-indegree queue represent?

options.text: Vertices whose currently remaining prerequisites are all satisfied.
Vertices that still have at least one unprocessed prerequisite.
Vertices already emitted from the result.
Vertices proven to belong to a cycle.

feedback.reason: Zero remaining indegree is the readiness condition.

blocks.text: The frontier contains candidates that can be emitted without violating incoming dependencies. Emitting one may make more vertices ready.

items.prompt: How does Kahn's algorithm detect that a nonempty dependency graph has a cycle?

options.text: The emitted result contains fewer vertices than the graph.
The queue becomes longer than the edge list.
Every vertex has equal indegree and outdegree.
The first processed edge proves a cycle.

feedback.reason: A cyclic residual subgraph has no vertex that can be emitted.

blocks.text: If the algorithm stops before outputting all vertices, remaining vertices are blocked by dependencies in a cycle. A complete output of all vertices is the acyclic case.

Always place the alphabetically smaller vertex first.
They must be adjacent in the output.
They must occupy the same position.

feedback.reason: Topological order constrains dependencies, not unrelated vertices.

blocks.text: Independent vertices can be interleaved or swapped as long as every directed edge points from an earlier prerequisite to a later dependent.
